strengths: Addresses a clearly novel and timely problem (watermarking diffusion language models), which is the first serious attempt at this and identifies a fundamental limitation (lack of context availability) that naive adaptations of ARLM watermarks suffer from.

Principled theoretical framework: formulates DLM watermarking as a constrained optimization problem (maximizing expected green ratio subject to a KL constraint), and derives a closed-form/implicit solution (Theorem 3.1) with rigorous proof in the appendix.

Elegant and satisfying theoretical interpretation: the resulting scheme decomposes into an 'expectation boost' and 'predictive bias' term, and is shown to exactly recover standard Red-Green ARLM watermarks in the autoregressive special case, unifying prior and new work.

Practical, efficient instantiation: derives closed-form/efficient computation of the hash distribution for SumHash (via FFT-based convolution) and MinHash, keeping the algorithm computationally tractable (minimal generation overhead, shown empirically in App. H.1).

Detector is unchanged from prior Red-Green watermarks, which is a nice compatibility/simplicity property and inherits known statistical guarantees (further refined via more rigorous binomial test derivation using i.i.d. Bernoulli green lists in App. F, with proofs).

Extensive empirical evaluation across two DLM backbones (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B), multiple hash schemes, context sets, remasking strategies, temperatures, number of diffusion steps, and an infilling-specific model (DreamOn), consistently showing >99% TPR@1%FPR with minimal quality degradation.

Strong set of ablations isolating the contribution of each design component (expectation boost vs. predictive bias, iterations, parameterization, top-k, gamma, green list distribution) that support the optimization framework's necessity.

Robustness evaluation against a reasonably broad set of attacks (deletion, substitution, context-aware substitution, paraphrasing, back-translation) and favorable comparison against order-agnostic baselines (Unigram, PatternMark) and other ARLM watermark adaptations (AAR, KTH).
Good reproducibility: detailed experimental setup, hyperparameters, and code release.
weaknesses: The optimization formulation relies on a KL-divergence constraint as a proxy for quality, which the paper itself shows (Sec 4.3) is a poor proxy in practice (epsilon-parameterization performs much worse than delta-parameterization) -- this somewhat undermines the theoretical elegance/motivation of the constrained optimization framing, since the practical algorithm essentially abandons the principled constraint in favor of an ad hoc constant.

Security analysis is relatively shallow: the paper asserts that using the same detector as Red-Green watermarks gives 'similar security', but does not empirically evaluate scrubbing/spoofing/watermark-stealing attacks (e.g., analogues of Jovanović et al. 2024 or Zhang et al. 2024) specifically against the proposed DLM watermark, despite citing this as a known vulnerability of low-context-size Red-Green schemes.

Quality evaluation relies primarily on perplexity (measured via an external LLM) and a single GPT-4o-as-judge score; there is no human evaluation, and perplexity is a known imperfect measure of generation quality, especially for the multi-directional diffusion generation process.

The theoretical decomposition and closed-form derivations (Sec 3.3) are presented for a simplified special case (SumHash, C={-1}), and while App I.2 generalizes it, the intuitive interpretation for general hash functions/contexts used in main experiments (e.g., C={-1,1}) is less transparently connected to the two-term story in the main text.

Robustness to strong adversarial attacks (paraphrasing, back-translation) still degrades notably at shorter sequence lengths, and the paper does not compare its robustness quantitatively and directly against strong ARLM watermark robustness numbers under identical conditions, making it hard to assess whether 'similar robustness to existing ARLM watermarks' is fully substantiated.

The comparison with order-agnostic watermarks (Unigram, PatternMark) is relegated to the appendix, though it is an important baseline category directly relevant to the DLM setting; its placement may underweight this comparison's importance for readers skimming the main paper.

Evaluation is limited to two model families (LLaDA, Dream) and general instruction-following/infilling tasks; there is no evaluation on code generation or more structured tasks where diffusion LMs are also being deployed, which limits generality claims somewhat.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and timely problem: no prior work provides a practical watermark for diffusion language models (DLMs), which generate tokens in arbitrary (non-autoregressive) order, making standard Red-Green hashing inapplicable.

Provides a principled theoretical framework: watermarking is cast as a constrained optimization problem (maximize expected green ratio subject to a per-token KL constraint), with a closed-form implicit solution (Theorem 3.1) derived via Lagrangian/KKT analysis.

Nicely shows that the proposed scheme reduces exactly to the standard ARLM Red-Green watermark when restricted to the autoregressive setting (Sec. 3.3, App. E), lending credibility to the generalization.
Keeps the detector identical to existing Red-Green detectors, which is practically convenient and preserves existing security/robustness properties of that detector family.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two DLM backbones (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) and an infilling-specialized model (DreamOn-7B), multiple hash schemes (SumHash, MinHash), multiple context sizes, remasking strategies, temperatures, and diffusion step counts.
Reasonably thorough robustness analysis against word deletion/substitution, context-aware substitution, paraphrasing, and back-translation, showing graceful degradation with sequence length.

Good reproducibility effort: code release, detailed appendix with hyperparameters, proofs, statistical justification of the binomial test under i.i.d. green-list sampling (App. F), and runtime/overhead analysis showing minimal generation overhead.
weaknesses: The primary comparison in the main text (Sec. 4.1) is against a 'naive' baseline that only watermarks tokens with fully unmasked context -- a fairly weak strawman. The more competitive order-agnostic baselines (Unigram, PatternMark) are relegated to the appendix, where the performance gap is noticeably smaller, especially outside the low-distortion regime, which somewhat undercuts the headline '>99% TPR, highly superior' framing in the main paper.

Quality evaluation relies primarily on model self-perplexity (likely biased, since boosting likely tokens can keep perplexity low while still altering content) and GPT-4o-as-judge scores; there is no human evaluation to validate that the reported quality preservation holds for real users/readers.

The 'optimization problem' is solved only approximately in practice: a single first-order fixed-point iteration, a top-k truncation of the hash/token distributions, and a scalar δ-parameterization replacing the theoretically-justified ε-constraint (which is shown to actually perform worse). This means the elegant theory in Sec. 3.1 is substantially watered down in the practical algorithm, and the empirical gains are driven largely by heuristic choices rather than the optimization formalism itself.

No formal security/robustness analysis specific to the DLM setting (e.g., adaptive attacks that exploit non-autoregressive generation or the predictive-bias term) -- robustness claims mostly piggyback on known ARLM Red-Green properties rather than being newly established for this scheme.

Statistical validity of the detector (Appendix F) is shown to deviate from nominal normal/binomial assumptions when the hash space is small relative to sequence length, which could affect FPR calibration in some realistic low-vocabulary/short-context configurations, though the paper argues this is usually negligible.

Core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the method is essentially an 'expectation over context hash distribution' extension of the well-established Red-Green scheme, combined with a predictive-bias term; the conceptual leap, while useful, is more of a careful engineering adaptation than a fundamentally new watermarking paradigm.

Evaluation is restricted to two/three specific open-source DLM architectures (LLaDA, Dream family); generalizability to other diffusion LM paradigms (e.g., continuous-state diffusion, different masking schedules) is not demonstrated.

strengths: First systematic treatment of watermarking for diffusion language models (DLMs), addressing a clear gap given the rapid emergence of this model class and the inapplicability of standard ARLM hashing-based watermarks.

Principled theoretical framework: watermarking is cast as a constrained optimization problem (maximizing expected green ratio subject to a KL constraint), with a clean closed-form implicit solution (Theorem 3.1) and a clear connection back to standard Red-Green ARLM watermarks as a special case (Sec 3.3, App E), lending strong conceptual coherence to the method.

Practical, efficient instantiation: the paper shows how to compute the hash distribution efficiently (FFT-based convolution for SumHash, O(|C||Σ|) for MinHash) and provides a simple fixed-point/top-k algorithm with minimal computational overhead (Fig 17, App H.1).

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: multiple DLMs (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, DreamOn for infilling), multiple hashing schemes, multiple context sets, multiple remasking strategies, temperatures, number of diffusion steps, and thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each component (expectation boost vs predictive bias, iterations, parameterization).

Strong, consistent results: >99% TPR@1%FPR with minimal quality degradation, clearly outperforming naive baseline adaptations of ARLM watermarks as well as additional baselines (AAR, KTH) and prior order-agnostic watermarks (Unigram, PatternMark), with the latter comparison also addressing watermark security considerations.

Robustness analysis against both local edits (deletion, substitution, context-aware substitution) and stronger adversaries (paraphrasing, back-translation), showing behavior consistent with and comparable to established ARLM watermark robustness results.

High transparency and reproducibility: detailed appendices covering proofs, additional ablations, green-list distributional assumptions and their statistical implications (binomial vs hypergeometric), hash implementation equivalence to prior work, compute resources, and code availability.
The detector is unchanged from standard Red-Green ARLM watermarks, which is a practically appealing design choice since it preserves known statistical guarantees and ease of adoption/integration.
weaknesses: The method inherits the same security weaknesses as Red-Green ARLM watermarks (e.g., watermark stealing/scrubbing attacks), especially for small context sizes; while acknowledged, no new mitigation or deeper security analysis specific to the DLM setting is provided.
Evaluation is restricted to two (three, including DreamOn) open-source DLM families; generality to other emerging DLM architectures/training objectives is not established.

The quality evaluation relies substantially on perplexity (via an external LM) and GPT-4o-as-judge scores, both of which have known biases/limitations as quality proxies, and no human evaluation is included.

The KL-constrained (ε-parameterization) variant, which is the theoretically principled solution to the stated optimization problem, is empirically shown to perform worse than the heuristic δ-parameterization, suggesting the optimization framework's practical value is somewhat undercut by its own tightest theoretical instantiation, and the explanation given is only intuitive/anecdotal rather than rigorously analyzed.

The top-k approximation and single-iteration fixed-point simplification, while empirically justified, mean the actual deployed algorithm deviates noticeably from the theoretical solution, slightly weakening the tightness of the link between theory and practice.

Robustness results against strong adversaries (paraphrasing, back-translation) show substantial degradation at shorter lengths, and the paper does not explore more adaptive or watermark-aware attacks tailored to the DLM setting specifically.

strengths: Tackles a novel and timely problem: the first watermarking scheme specifically designed for diffusion language models (DLMs), addressing the real limitation that ARLM watermarks depend on sequential context unavailable in DLM generation.

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper formulates watermarking as a constrained optimization problem (maximizing expected green-ratio subject to a KL constraint), derives an implicit closed-form solution (Theorem 3.1), and shows the scheme reduces exactly to standard Red-Green ARLM watermarks in the autoregressive special case, providing a principled and elegant unifying framework.

Clear and intuitive decomposition of the resulting algorithm into 'expectation boost' and 'predictive bias' terms, which aids understanding of why the method works and is empirically validated via component ablations.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation across two DLM backbones (LLADA-8B, DREAM-7B), multiple hashing schemes (SumHash, MinHash), multiple context sets, multiple remasking strategies (uniform, entropy-based, block/autoregressive), temperatures, and an infilling-specific model (DREAMON-V0-7B), consistently showing >99% TPR@1%FPR with minimal quality degradation.

Thorough comparison against relevant baselines (naive ARLM adaptation, AAR, KTH, GaussMark, Unigram, PatternMark), including a careful statistical critique of Unigram's lack of Type-1 error control and vulnerability to spoofing/scrubbing, backed by dedicated empirical FPR-calibration experiments (Fig. 7, Table 2).

Robustness evaluations against realistic attacks (deletion, substitution, context-aware substitution, paraphrasing, back-translation) show the watermark retains strong detectability, with a compelling explanation (expectation-boosting) for why it is even more robust to context-aware substitution than standard schemes.

Careful attention to statistical soundness of the detector (i.i.d. vs correlated Bernoulli green lists, binomial vs hypergeometric tests) with theoretical derivations and simulations (Appendix F) that improve rigor over prior Red-Green implementations.

Practical considerations are addressed: computational overhead is analyzed and shown to be minimal, with both a general and an optimized implementation validated to be equivalent; code is released for reproducibility.

Comprehensive appendix with numerous ablations (top-k, gamma, green-list distribution, number of diffusion steps, self-hashing) that substantially strengthen confidence in the robustness of the core claims.
weaknesses: The KL-constrained optimization formulation (Eq. 1) is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be an imperfect proxy for text quality (Sec 4.3), and the recommended delta-parameterization abandons the theoretical guarantees of Theorem 3.1 in practice, somewhat undercutting the significance of the formal optimization framework as the practical driver of results.

Benchmark accuracy results (Table 1, Table 3) show that in some model/hyperparameter combinations (e.g., LLADA-8B) the naive baseline actually preserves accuracy better than the proposed watermark despite much lower TPR, indicating the quality-detectability tradeoff is not uniformly favorable and warrants more nuanced guidance for practitioners.

The security analysis is somewhat limited to citing prior work (Jovanovic et al.) for low-context vulnerability to spoofing/scrubbing; no new empirical spoofing/scrubbing attack experiments specifically targeting the proposed scheme are conducted in this paper, despite this being highlighted as an advantage over Unigram/PatternMark.

Robustness to paraphrasing/back-translation, while improving with sequence length, still degrades substantially compared to local edits, and the paper does not explore mitigations or provide strong guidance on minimum practical sequence lengths for robust deployment against these more realistic LLM-based attacks.

Evaluation is restricted to two open-source DLM backbones and a fairly narrow set of tasks (long-form QA style prompts plus one infilling case); generalization to a broader range of DLM architectures, larger scales, or more diverse downstream tasks (e.g., code generation, multimodal DLMs) is not demonstrated.

The interpretability decomposition (expectation boost / predictive bias) is derived explicitly only for the simple SumHash with C={-1} case in the main text, with generalization deferred to the appendix, which may limit intuitive accessibility for more complex/general hash and context configurations used elsewhere in the experiments.

strengths: Addresses a novel and timely problem: no prior watermark had been designed for diffusion language models (DLMs), and the paper convincingly motivates why ARLM watermarks fail when applied naively (context tokens not yet generated).

Principled theoretical framework: watermarking is cast as a constrained optimization problem (maximizing expected green ratio subject to a KL constraint), with an implicit closed-form solution (Theorem 3.1) and a clean reduction showing that, in the autoregressive limit, the scheme recovers exactly the Red-Green watermark — a nice unifying result.

Detector compatibility: the proposed scheme keeps the exact same (well-understood, statistically grounded) binomial detector as standard Red-Green watermarks, which is practically appealing and avoids introducing new detection machinery.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two DLM backbones (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) and an infilling-specialized model (DreamOn-v0-7B), multiple hashing schemes, context sizes, remasking strategies, temperatures, and numbers of diffusion steps, with many ablations in the appendix.

Reasonably thorough baseline comparisons (naive ARLM adaptation, AAR, KTH, GaussMark, Unigram, PatternMark) and a careful, somewhat novel analysis showing Unigram/PatternMark have poor Type-1 error control and security vulnerabilities that the proposed method avoids.

Robustness evaluation against deletions, substitutions, context-aware substitutions, paraphrasing, and back-translation, which is standard practice in the watermarking literature and appropriately included here.
Runtime/complexity analysis and an optimized implementation showing the overhead can be made comparable to ARLM watermarks, plus a clearly documented reproducibility appendix.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an extension/generalization of the existing Red-Green watermark machinery to handle uncertain context via expectation; while the derivation is non-trivial, the conceptual novelty beyond prior ARLM watermark theory is incremental.

Benchmark-accuracy results (Table 1, Table 3) are inconsistent: for LLaDA-8B, the weaker (lower-TPR) baseline sometimes retains notably higher downstream task accuracy than the proposed method, undercutting the abstract's claim of "minimal quality impact" and suggesting the quality picture is more nuanced/mixed than advertised.

The optimization formulation implicitly assumes the whole sequence is sampled at once from q*, and the appendix ablation (Fig. 9) shows watermark strength degrades as the number of diffusion steps increases (closer to realistic multi-step generation), indicating a non-trivial theory-practice gap that is acknowledged but not deeply resolved.

Quality is evaluated mainly via perplexity (using an external LLM) and an LLM-as-judge score with GPT-4o; robustness/paraphrasing attacks also rely on closed, versioned proprietary models (e.g., "GPT5-MINI", "GPT5-NANO") that are not citable/fixed artifacts, which raises reproducibility concerns as these APIs change or become unavailable over time.

Security analysis (robustness to spoofing/scrubbing) for the proposed watermark itself is thin — mostly deferred to citing prior work's findings on context-size vulnerability, without a dedicated empirical security evaluation analogous to the Unigram/PatternMark analysis provided.

Robustness to strong adversaries (paraphrasing, back-translation) degrades substantially at shorter sequence lengths (TPR dropping well below practical thresholds at ~50 tokens), which may limit real-world applicability for shorter generations.

The main (non-optimized) implementation incurs measurable generation overhead, and matching baseline speed requires a bespoke, model-specific optimized implementation that is not the one used for most reported experiments, somewhat limiting the generality claimed.

strengths: Addresses a novel and timely problem: watermarking diffusion language models, which is an emerging LLM paradigm not covered by existing ARLM watermarking schemes.

Provides a principled theoretical framework (constrained optimization over expected green ratio with KL constraint) that yields a practical algorithm and provably recovers standard Red-Green ARLM watermarks as a special case, giving strong conceptual grounding.
The decomposition into 'expectation boost' and 'predictive bias' terms gives intuitive interpretability to the proposed method, and is nicely illustrated in Fig. 1.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: multiple DLMs (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, DreamOn for infilling), multiple hash schemes, remasking strategies, context sizes, temperatures, number of diffusion steps, and quality metrics (perplexity, GPT-4o judge, benchmark accuracy).

Strong comparisons against relevant baselines (naive ARLM adaptation, Unigram, PatternMark, AAR, KTH, GaussMark), consistently showing the proposed method dominates in detectability/quality trade-off.

Careful statistical treatment of the detector (i.i.d. Bernoulli green list vs correlated, exact hypergeometric/binomial tests, Type-1 error control analysis for Unigram vs. proposed method), which strengthens the reliability claims.

Robustness evaluation against deletion, substitution, context-aware substitution, paraphrasing, and back-translation attacks, showing the watermark retains reasonable detectability, including a nice explanation of why context-aware substitution robustness emerges naturally from the expectation formulation.
Thorough appendix with proofs, additional ablations, runtime analysis showing minimal overhead, and an optimized implementation validated to match the main implementation.
Reproducibility details and code release are provided.
weaknesses: The security analysis of the proposed watermark against targeted spoofing/scrubbing attacks (beyond citing prior scrubbing/spoofing results on Red-Green schemes) is somewhat limited; the paper acknowledges vulnerability at low context size but does not extensively test watermark stealing attacks directly on the DLM setting.
The fixed-point iteration lacks theoretical convergence guarantees, and while empirically one iteration suffices, this is a heuristic choice not fully justified analytically.

Benchmark accuracy results (Table 1, App C.5) show inconsistent trends across models (e.g., LLaDA-8B baseline sometimes has smaller accuracy drop despite much lower TPR), which is acknowledged but not fully resolved — it leaves some ambiguity about utility trade-offs in practice.
The top-k approximation and other approximations (e.g., restricting hash context to small C) could have further impact on worst-case adversarial robustness not fully explored.
Evaluation relies mostly on two DLM backbones (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B) and one infilling model; broader coverage of diverse DLM architectures/sizes would strengthen generality claims.

The δ vs ε parameterization analysis reveals that the theoretically principled KL-constrained version underperforms the heuristic δ-parameterization, suggesting the optimization framework's practical utility is somewhat limited relative to its theoretical appeal.
